title: We stopped treating AI NPCs as chat sessions. The hard part started after that.
author: ChemicalPresent8796
selftext:
Most AI-character systems are still basically a conversation window: you talk, the model answers, the session ends.

We wanted the character to keep existing.

In Virtual Twilight the characters have persistent memory, relationships, emotional state and world context across different experiences. You can talk to the same entity, leave, play something else with them, return later, and prior interactions still matter.

That immediately created harder design problems than prompting:
- what should actually be remembered?
- when should memories decay or be consolidated?
- how much autonomy is fun before it becomes annoying?
- what should happen while the player is offline?
- how do you keep the same character coherent across chat, 3D/WebXR, management, racing and rhythm games?
- how do you stop memory from becoming an infinite transcript?

We ended up building systems outside the LLM for persistent state, relationship logic, memory selection and autonomous behaviour.

The consumer sandbox is live here if anyone wants to poke at what we mean:
https://www.virtualtwilight.app/

I am much more interested in comparing architectures with other AI-game developers than doing a generic "check out my game" post. How are people here handling persistence and offline agent behaviour?

Disclosure: I am one of the people building Virtual Twilight / the underlying runtime.

comments.author: ericoinen
comments.body:
We came at the same problem from the game side, and the split that made it tractable was: the engine owns state, the model owns voice, and the two never swap jobs.

What gets remembered is not the conversation. Resolved events get remembered: a die result, an HP change, an item moving, a door that is now open. Those are rows the engine wrote, not sentences the model produced, so they can be queried, replayed, and shown to the player as-is. The prose that wrapped them is disposable and gets summarised hard. That dissolves the infinite transcript problem by never letting a transcript be the source of truth.

Decay gets easy once that split exists, because you are only deciding which prose to keep, and a wrong call there costs texture, not canon.

Offline behaviour we deliberately gave up. Clocks advance on turns, not on wall time. Anything that happens while the player is away has to be re-narrated to them when they come back, and the re-narration is exactly where a character stops feeling like the same character.

Cross-surface coherence turned out to be the boring answer: personality lives in a short hand-written sheet that is re-injected every call and never grows. Memory that grows is what makes characters drift. A fixed sheet plus queryable canon does not.

The game is Grimscribe, a solo browser RPG where an LLM is the dungeon master and a hardcoded rules engine owns every die roll, HP total, item and grid square. Last night's session ran twelve turns without a single die being thrown, because the engine refused every attack on reach or on turn order and the model had to narrate the refusals instead of writing a hit. That is the run that tells you the split is real, and it is the thing I would ask your system too: what does it do when the character wants something the world does not allow?

https://grimscribe.win

replies.author: ChemicalPresent8796
replies.body:
This is very close to the boundary we ended up with too.

Intent can be probabilistic, execution cannot.

The character can want to do something, reason about doing it and even become frustrated when it cannot — but the world/action layer still decides whether the action is actually valid.

So if the NPC wants to enter a locked location, attack someone it cannot reach, use an object it does not possess, etc., the model does not get to rewrite reality. The action fails or gets rejected and the character has to react/re-plan from that state.

Where we differ slightly is that we keep more psychological state persistent too: relationships, motivation, emotion, memory importance, personality-weighted recall etc.

I really like your “transcript is not canon” formulation though. That is basically the same reason we moved memory outside the conversation context.
